title: French Open Media Boycott: Top Players Unite in Pay Dispute
summary: The usually glitzy pre-tournament media day at the French Open took a tense turn on Friday when top players staged a coordinated protest over pay. Aryna Sabalenka, the outspoken world number two from Belarus, cut her news conference to just 10 minutes, while men's number one Jannik Sinner and four-time champion Iga Swiatek followed suit. The 'work-to-rule' directive—doing only the contractual minimum—was a collective jab at the four Grand Slam tournaments, which players argue keep too much of the revenue for themselves. 'We just wanted to make our point and we are united,' Sabalenka told reporters. '15 minutes is better than zero.' The 28-year-old has been a leading voice in the dispute, recently warning that players might boycott a Grand Slam 'at some point.' Coco Gauff, the reigning women's champion, said she was proud of the solidarity in an individual sport. Taylor Fritz, the American world number eight, explained they acted because they 'felt ignored.' Notably, Novak Djokovic, a 24-time major winner and longtime advocate for players' rights, did not participate but voiced support. 'I have always been on the players' side,' he said, adding that very few people actually earn a living from professional tennis. The protest is the latest in a long-running battle over prize money distribution. While Grand Slams generate billions, players argue the percentage allocated to them hasn't kept pace. By limiting media commitments—a crucial part of the sport's promotion—the stars are leveraging their visibility to force a conversation. Whether this tactic will pressure organizers remains to be seen, but the message is clear: the players are done being ignored.
why_it_matters: This protest shows how even athletes in an individual sport can use their collective influence to challenge powerful institutions, a lesson in labor rights and the economics of entertainment that echoes far beyond tennis.

background_read: In 1973, men's tennis players boycotted Wimbledon to support their union, leading to the formation of the ATP; this protest shows that collective action in tennis has a long history.
The four Grand Slam tournaments—Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, US Open—generate billions of dollars in revenue from tickets, sponsorships, and broadcasting rights.
Novak Djokovic co-founded the Professional Tennis Players Association (PTPA) in 2020 to give players more say in how the sport is run, since they are independent contractors and not employees.

Tennis players often earn very little early in their careers; only a small percentage make enough prize money to cover travel and coaching, which is one reason lower-ranked players strongly support better revenue sharing.
Limiting media access strikes at the promotional side of the sport, because star players attract viewers and sponsors, making their silence a powerful bargaining tool.

perspectives.description: By uniting, the stars amplify their voices and could win a fairer share of revenue, helping not just top earners but the hundreds of lower-ranked players who struggle to cover costs.
Cutting media time might reduce the tournament's promotional reach, which ultimately lowers the overall money pot—hurting the same players they want to help if sponsors or broadcasters lose interest.

Grand Slams are non-profit organizations that reinvest income into developing tennis, stadium upgrades, and grassroots programs, making the tension between athlete pay and the sport's long-term health a complex puzzle.
If players escalate to a full Grand Slam boycott, the tournaments could be forced to negotiate a binding revenue-sharing model, similar to strikes in team sports like the NBA or the Premier League.
